prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run in this world yet, and the starting network scores 0. Across past searches, only one design ever scored above 0. It feeds the legal-action mask in as input channels under four layouts (as given, transposed, y-flipped, x-flipped) and sums four per-type output maps put back into those same layouts. My reading is that the world's action indexing may differ from its description, and the mask is the only input written in the world's real action order, so the network can learn which layout is correct. Changing only the recipe never helped any other network. So all three candidates use the four-layout design. The first reproduces it as the baseline for this world. The second changes only the recipe (more samples, longer credit horizon), which has not been tried on a network that works. The third adds trunk depth and feeds the mask into the heads. All three are estimated to cost at most as much compute as the starting network, so none loses training steps.

### Round 2
All four trials so far scored 0, including the four-layout design, which scored 0.22 in another world. Late training success was also 0 in every run, so no signal has appeared at all. Earlier searches showed that different worlds break the stated action layout in different ways, and hedges that covered only one deviation failed. The four-layout design covers flips and one transpose of a type-major index order (type outermost, then position), but not other orderings. Two untested deviations are plausible: a position-major index order (a = cell*T + type), and DONE placed first instead of last. Both would scramble the alignment between the mask's index order and the grid. The trunk's 1x1 stem and 3x3 convs already absorb channel reordering and anchor offsets of one cell. So this round widens the hedge: all 4 flip combinations × 2 axis orders × 2 type orders = 16 layouts. One candidate adds a DONE-first hedge and one gets more samples. If everything stays at 0, the deviation lies outside the action layout.

### Round 3
Six trials have all scored zero. The best was 0.002 on one seed, which is only 1 build in 512 and is noise. Late training success was 0 in every trial. Feeding the mask in under 16 layouts covers every flip and transpose between the mask and the grid, in both type-major and position-major order, and it still failed. Moving DONE to the front, 2 PPO epochs and a deeper trunk also failed. So in this world the problem is probably not how the mask lines up with the grid. Two untested explanations remain. (1) The observation tensor may be stored in a different memory order, such as [Y,X,C] read as [C,Y,X]. A 1x1 convolution cannot undo that, so every network would fail. (2) Badly scaled returns may make the critic's gradients swamp the shared trunk under the fixed gradient-norm clip. Each of the first two candidates tests one of these on the 16-layout network. The third combines both, to find out whether any nonzero signal exists before the final round.

### Round 4
After 9 trials, only the 16-layout mask network (r2c1) has scored above 0 on dev: 0.002 on one seed, 0.000 on the other. Separately, r3c1 reached a late training success of 0.0003. Both are within noise, but no other trial has shown any signal. The 16 layouts cover every flip and transpose of the grid in both type-first and position-first action order, so a mismatch in action indexing is probably no longer the main problem. Other things that also scored 0: obs memory order (r3c1), a separate critic (r3c2), both together (r3c3), DONE placed first (r2c3), and 2 PPO epochs (r1c2, r2c2). Learning itself now looks like the bottleneck. This is the last round, and any 2-seed mean of 0.002 or more beats r2c1. I propose three tests on the 16-layout network: more trunk depth for reasoning about heights; twice as many PPO updates at the same sample count; and footprint pooling done inside each layout's own index frame, a structural fit to how bricks land.

name: 16-layout mask, default recipe
hypothesis: Extends the four-layout design to 16 layouts: type-major and position-major indexing, each in (y,x) or (x,y) axis order, each under all 4 flip combinations. If this world indexes actions position-major or with a 180° rotation, only this broader hedge can align the mask with the grid. Refuted if both seeds score 0 and late training success is 0.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and

reply.evidence: The text never says the target channels are shifted or rolled along x. Most of it is about action-index layouts (Rounds 1–2: flips, transposes, "position-major", "DONE placed first"). The closest it gets is Round 3: "The observation tensor may be stored in a different memory order, such as [Y,X,C] read as [C,Y,X]." That is a guess about how the whole tensor is stored. It is not a 4-column wrap-around shift of the target, missing, extra and height channels.
